crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 3 · Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio (6L² vs L³)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why Elephants Have Huge Ears & Cells Stay Microscopic (SA:V Scaling)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: When a cell or organism enlarges by linear scale factor k, its surface area grows as k² while its metabolising volume grows as k³ — so SA/V = 6/L drops inversely with size.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: SA = 6L²,   V = L³   ⇒   SA : V = 6 / L
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: If a cubical cell doubles its side length from L = 1 μm to L = 2 μm (k = 2), by what factor does its Surface-Area-to-Volume ratio change?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Surface area multiplies by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so SA:V halves from 6:1 to 3:1.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 13 · Mendel's Punnett Squares & Clinical Screening
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Punnett Grids Are 2×2 Area Diagrams & Medical Tests Obey Bayes' Rule
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A Punnett square for Aa × Aa is literally the algebraic expansion (0.5A + 0.5a)² = 0.25AA + 0.50Aa + 0.25aa, and genetic carrier screening relies on Bayes' theorem.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: In a cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), given that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype (AA or Aa), what is the conditional probability it is a carrier (Aa)?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Out of 3 dominant-phenotype boxes (1 AA and 2 Aa), 2 are Aa, so P(Aa | Dominant) = 2/3.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Physics Ch 1 · Kinematics (Velocity Slope & Displacement Area)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Velocity Is the Derivative of Position; Displacement Is the Area Under v(t)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: On a distance-time graph, gradient Δs/Δt is speed. On a speed-time graph, the area of the trapezium under v(t) is distance travelled s = v₀t + ½at².
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: v(t) = ds/dt,   Δs = ∫ v(t) dt = v₀t + ½at²
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: A train accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over 8 seconds. Using the trapezium area under v(t), how far does it travel?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Resolving Forces on a Ramp with Unit-Circle Sine & Cosine Shadows

schoolQuestions.prompt: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 72 and 120 using prime factorisation, and verify that HCF × LCM = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1 (Prime Factor Trees): 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3¹ × 5¹.
Step 2 (Venn Intersection = HCF): Take min powers: 2³ × 3¹ = 24.
Step 3 (Venn Union = LCM): Take max powers: 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360.
Step 4 (Invariant Check): 24 × 360 = 8640 = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: HCF = 24 and LCM = 360 because 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; their overlap is 2³ × 3 = 24 and their union is 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

polyaStages.title: 1. Understand the Problem
polyaStages.subtitle: Isolate the unknown, the given data, and the governing condition
prompts: What is the unknown? Can I name it or draw it as a Singapore bar segment?
What are the data and units? Are any quantities hidden in words like 'bisects', 'regular', or 'independent'?
What is the invariant condition linking the data to the unknown? Is it enough to determine the unknown?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: A train passes a 300 m platform in 24 seconds and passes a standing lamp-post in 9 seconds at constant speed. Find the length of the train.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Unknown: Train length L. Data: Lamp-post time = 9 s (covers L only); Platform time = 24 s (covers L + 300 m). Invariant: Speed v is constant!

polyaStages.title: 2. Devise a Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Select a heuristic: Draw a Bar Model, Try a Simpler Case, Work Backwards, or Look for Symmetry
prompts: Can I draw a Concrete → Pictorial bar model or auxiliary geometric line?
What happens in a tiny case (n = 1, 2, 3) — does a pattern of differences emerge?
Can I work backwards from the target or use an extreme case (h → 0, θ = 0° or 90°)?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Compare the two journeys of the train on a single Singapore distance bar.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Draw two bars: Bar 1 = [Train L] takes 9 s. Bar 2 = [Train L] + [300 m] takes 24 s. The extra 300 m alone takes 24 − 9 = 15 s!

polyaStages.title: 3. Carry Out the Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Execute each algebraic or geometric step and check that every step is reversible
prompts: Can I prove that each step follows from the line above it?
Did I keep units and signs consistent across every operation?
Can I see the geometric meaning of the intermediate number?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Compute the train's speed from the 15-second difference and find L.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Speed v = 300 m ÷ 15 s = 20 m/s. Since passing the lamp-post takes 9 s, Train length L = 20 m/s × 9 s = 180 m.

polyaStages.title: 4. Look Back & Generalise
polyaStages.subtitle: Sanity-check dimensions, test a second method, and turn the result into a reusable formula
prompts: Does the answer survive a substitution check in the original problem?
Can I derive the general formula for any platform length P and times t₁, t₂?
Where else can I use this 'subtract the two states to isolate the difference' trick?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Verify L = 180 m and write the universal formula.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Check: (180 + 300) m ÷ 20 m/s = 480 ÷ 20 = 24 s ✓. General Formula: L = P · t₁ / (t₂ − t₁).

visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The two staircases interlock into a solid rectangle of width n and height (n + 1)!

visualMathTips.title: Why a Circle's Area Is πr²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Slice a circle into 24 pizza sectors and comb them together alternating up and down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The wavy top and bottom each use half the circumference (πr), while the height is the radius r — forming a rectangle of base πr and height r!

visualMathTips.title: Why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for Every Angle
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: On the @saxster/atlas unit circle of radius 1, level light casts vertical shadow sin θ and top light casts horizontal shadow cos θ.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Those two shadows are the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 — so their squares always add to 1² = 1!

visualMathTips.title: Why a 95% Accurate Test Can Be 72% Wrong
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: In the @saxster/atlas 1,000-person unit square at 2% prevalence, only 20 people are sick while 980 are healthy.

visualMathTips.title: Why Slope and Area Are Inverses (FTC)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Compare the blue triangle of area under f′(t) = t with the red height bar of f(x) = ½x².
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Each thin strip of area f′(t)·dt equals df — the tiny vertical step of the original curve. Summing all tiny rises gives total height f(x) − f(0)!

visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Drag the red basis vector Aî = (a, c) and blue basis vector Aĵ = (b, d) in the @saxster/atlas 2×2 Matrix Sandbox.
